metadata.title: It's Not That. It's This.
metadata.purpose: Teach viewers to recognize negative parallelism and other AI writing tells, then fix them with an anti-ai-writing-style.md file in Claude Cowork.
metadata.clock: narration (Kokoro) — durations are word-count estimates until GATE 0 audio lock

props.command: What is: It's Not That. It's This?

beats.narration_text: Ahoj. This is Liam, in for Bear. One sentence — and I already know you used AI. How? It starts with 'It's not this, it's that.' That pattern is everywhere. Let's tear it apart.

props.ask: How do I know you used AI to write this?
props.answer_preview: You said 'It's not X, it's Y.' Every LLM writes it.

beats.narration_text: Negative parallelism. 'It's not a tool — it's a collaborator.' 'Not just deployments — also compliance.' Every LLM reaches for this pattern by default. Cisco. Accenture. McKinsey. Workday. Satya Nadella. All caught using it in official communications.

card.sub: The signature AI tell now saturating corporate writing — caught in filings from Cisco, Accenture, McKinsey, and more.

beats.narration_text: The pattern has fifteen disguises. 'This isn't X, this is Y.' 'Not X. Y.' 'Forget X. This is Y.' 'Less X, more Y.' 'X is dead. Y is the future.' 'You don't need X. You need Y.' And the sneakier ones — 'Sure, X works. But Y is where the real magic is.' All the same move. All instantly readable as machine output.

illustration.concept: 15 shapes of negative parallelism laid out as a pattern taxonomy
illustration.layout: 3-column grid of labelled phrase variants with the core 'It's not X, it's Y' structure highlighted at top

beats.narration_text: But negative parallelism isn't alone. There are eight more tells. Rule of three. Puffery. The participle trap. False ranges. Elegant variation. Copulative avoidance — AI never just says 'is.' Title case headers. And metronome rhythm — every sentence the same length, every paragraph three sentences.

illustration.concept: 8 additional AI writing tells displayed as a labelled list with short examples for each
illustration.layout: 2-column layout, tell name left, example phrase right, alternating warm ink and terracotta labels

beats.narration_text: The fix is one file. An anti-ai-writing-style.md you drop into your Claude Cowork folder. It contains the banned patterns, a hundred-plus banned words like 'delve,' 'unlock,' 'leverage,' pacing rules, and an anti-overfitting guide so Claude doesn't swing too far the other way.

card.sub: anti-ai-writing-style.md — banned patterns, banned vocab, pacing rules, anti-overfitting guide.

beats.narration_text: Setup is three steps. Create the file. Upload it into your Claude Cowork folder — alongside your about-me and my-company files. Then update your Global Instructions to tell Claude always to read it. After that, every session runs through it automatically.

illustration.concept: Cowork folder structure showing about-me, my-company, and anti-ai-writing-style files with an arrow indicating auto-read on session start
illustration.layout: vertical folder tree left side, annotation arrows pointing to each file on the right

beats.narration_text: Treat the file as a living document. AI writing patterns drift. Words that passed in 2024 read robotic now. Every three months: reread your last ten AI drafts, circle what sounds machine-written on second look, add it to the banned list. The file is your taste in text form.

card.sub: Update the file every 3 months. Patterns drift. Your banned list is your editorial judgment, captured.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Open your Claude Cowork folder right now. Create a file called anti-ai-writing-style.md. Add one rule you know you break. Just one. Run your next piece of writing through it and see what changes.

card.sub: Add one rule you know you break. Run your next draft through it.

beats.narration_text: Stop using the pattern. Ban it. Burn it. One file changes everything. This is Liam, in for Bear.

card.sub: this is Liam, in for Bear

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: your Claude-drafted content sounds like AI wrote it — over-structured, hedged, generic. Ask Claude to show you the specific phrases and patterns that mark text as AI-generated, the rewrite moves that eliminate them without losing the substance, and how to write a Claude prompt that produces less AI-sounding output from the start rather than fixing it afterward.
